questions.q: According to the chapter, which was the earliest form of exchange?
questions.a: The barter system: the chapter calls it the earliest form of exchange, with evidence from around the world.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what is the name for a piece of business done between people, especially an act of buying or selling?
questions.a: A transaction: the chapter's glossary defines it as a piece of business done between people, especially an act of buying or selling.

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with its description in Column II.
Column I: 1. Rai stones  2. Tajadero  3. Tevau  4. Money
Column II: P. A coil made from red birds' feathers, used on the Solomon Islands  Q. Giant discs of rock used on Yap Island  R. The common tool that everybody accepts to make or receive payments  S. A copper 'chopping knife' used in Central Mexico and parts of Central America
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Rai stones = giant rock discs of Yap Island; Tajadero = the Aztec copper chopping knife of Central Mexico; Tevau = the red feather coil of the Solomon Islands; money = the common tool everybody accepts for payments.

questions.q: Define the barter system. Give one example of barter of your own (not the chapter's eraser-and-pencil example).
questions.a: The barter system is a way of exchanging goods and services without using money. Example: a gardener gives a basket of guavas to a neighbour and takes a bottle of home-made pickle in return.
s: Defines barter as exchanging goods or services without using money
Gives a correct example of their own where goods or services are swapped with no money

questions.q: True or False? 'Under barter, people exchanged only crops and things they had made; animals were never used in exchange.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter lists cattle (cows, goats, horses, sheep) among the commodities people used in exchange, along with cowrie shells, salt, tea, tobacco, cloth and seeds.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: cattle such as cows, goats, horses and sheep were among the commodities used in exchange

questions.q: Answer briefly from the chapter: (a) What are commodities? (b) Name any two commodities, other than cattle, that people used for exchange under barter. (c) Besides coins and notes, what do people use today for transactions, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) Commodities are products or goods that can be traded, bought and sold. (b) Any two of: cowrie shells, salt, tea, tobacco, cloth, seeds. (c) Their mobile phones and computers.
s: Explains commodities as products or goods that can be traded, bought and sold
Names two commodities from the chapter's list, such as salt and cloth
States that people also use mobile phones and computers for transactions

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
I. Under barter, a service could be exchanged for goods.
II. The Tevau used on the Solomon Islands was a coil made from birds' feathers.
III. The chapter says barter came into use only after coins became hard to carry.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. The chapter says people exchanged goods or services for other goods and services, and the Tevau is a red feather coil; III is wrong because barter was the earliest form of exchange, before coins.

questions.q: In a hill village where nobody uses money, a mason repairs the headman's roof and takes two goats in return. A visitor writes, 'No exchange took place here, because no money was paid.' Which correction fits the chapter?
o: An exchange did take place: a service was traded for goods, which is barter
No exchange took place, because barter covers only goods traded for goods
It was only a gift, because goats were never used in exchange
It was a money payment, because goats are the village's currency notes
questions.a: An exchange did take place: barter is exchanging goods or services for other goods or services, so repair work traded for goats is barter. Goats are among the cattle the chapter lists as commodities.

questions.q: Kiran says, 'The Rai stones, the Tajadero and the Tevau prove that, all over the world, money has always been made of metal.' Do you agree? Give three reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. (1) Rai stones were giant discs of rock, not metal. (2) The Tevau was a coil of red birds' feathers; only the Tajadero was copper. (3) The commodities used in barter, such as cowrie shells, salt, tea and cloth, were not metal, and the chapter says the barter system used non-metallic money before coinage, which is metallic money.
s: Disagrees and shows Rai stones were rock, not metal
Shows the Tevau was made of feathers and only the Tajadero was copper
Uses the commodity list or the chapter's point that barter used non-metallic money before coinage

questions.q: The chapter defines money as 'the common tool that everybody accepts and uses in order to make or receive payments'. Use this definition to judge each of the following. (a) Cowrie shells in a region where all traders took them. (b) Goats in a village where everybody took them in payment, even though a goat cannot be split into parts. (c) A paper token Ravi draws at home, which only his own family will take. (d) Which of the three is weakest as money, and what does this tell you is the key test of money?
questions.a: (a) Cowrie shells can be money there, because all traders accepted them; the chapter lists them among items people used for exchange. (b) Goats can work as money in that village, because everybody accepted them for payments; the chapter lists cattle, including goats, among the commodities used for exchange, and being hard to divide does not stop something being accepted. (c) Ravi's token is not money, because only his family accepts it, not everybody. (d) The token is weakest; the key test is that everybody accepts it, not what it is made of or how easily it can be divided or carried.
s: Judges cowrie shells as money because all traders accepted them
Judges goats as money in that village because everybody accepted them, though they cannot be split
Rejects Ravi's token because only his family accepts it
Names the token as weakest and states that common acceptance is the key test

questions.q: What is the name for the situation in which two people each have exactly what the other wants and can exchange them directly?
questions.a: Double coincidence of wants.

questions.q: In the farmer's story, the wheat he got for his ox could not be stored for long because it would rot or be eaten by rats. Which problem of barter is this?
questions.a: Durability: the wheat cannot withstand damage, so it cannot be stored for a long time.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Under barter, a farmer cannot give only a part of his ox in exchange for a sweater.
Reason (R): An ox cannot be split into portions and still be useful, which is the problem of divisibility.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the ox cannot be divided, so part of it cannot be traded; the chapter calls this the problem of divisibility.

questions.q: Name the problem of barter shown in each case. (a) A fisherman's catch spoils in the heat before he finds anyone to trade with. (b) A man with one horse needs only a pair of slippers, but he cannot give half a horse.
questions.a: (a) Durability: the fish cannot be stored for long. (b) Divisibility: the horse cannot be split into a smaller part to match the slippers.
s: Names durability for the spoiling fish
Names divisibility for the horse that cannot be split

questions.q: Answer from the farmer's story in the chapter. (a) What did the farmer first exchange his ox for? (b) Name the three things he needed. (c) Why did he have to find a safe place for the leftover wheat?
questions.a: (a) Several bags of wheat. (b) A pair of new shoes, a sweater, and medicines for his grandmother. (c) The leftover wheat was all he had to trade the next time he needed something, so it had to be kept safe until then (and carried with him again).
s: States that the ox was exchanged for several bags of wheat
Names shoes, a sweater and medicines
Explains that the leftover wheat had to be kept for future exchanges

questions.q: Which of these situations shows the problem of portability rather than the problem of durability?
o: A salt trader must carry heavy sacks of salt over hills to every market
A milk seller's milk turns sour before he finds someone to trade with
A fruit grower's mangoes rot in his storeroom
A grain trader's stored rice is eaten by rats
questions.a: The salt trader carrying heavy sacks to every market: portability is about how easily goods can be carried or moved, while the other three are about goods that cannot be stored for long (durability).

questions.q: In a barter village, people agree by custom that 1 goat = 30 kg of rice and 1 blanket = 12 kg of rice. (a) How many blankets is one goat worth? (b) A herder needs only one blanket. Which problem of barter does he face, and why?
questions.a: (a) 30 / 12 = 2.5 blankets. (b) Divisibility: one goat is worth two and a half blankets, but he cannot give only part of a goat for one blanket.
s: Works out 30 / 12 = 2.5 blankets
Names divisibility: he cannot give part of a goat for one blanket

questions.q: Neel says, 'If the farmer finds one person who will give him shoes, a sweater and medicines, all for his ox, then every problem of barter is solved for him.' Is Neel right, wrong or partly right? Explain with the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Such a deal would meet the double coincidence of wants in one go and he would not have to carry wheat from place to place. But the chapter asks whether it would be easy to come across such a person: it is unlikely. Even then they must agree whether the ox is really worth all three things; with no common standard measure of value one side may feel it is a bad deal and refuse. And the next time he needs something, the same problems return.
s: Says partly right: one such deal meets the double coincidence of wants and saves carrying wheat
Notes that finding such a person is unlikely, as the chapter suggests
Shows that the lack of a common standard measure of value (or the next need) still remains

questions.q:
Read the case and answer.
Meenu lives in a coastal village where only barter is used. Each morning she catches about 12 kg of fish. She wants a cotton sari from a weaver who lives in a town 20 km inland, a sack of rice from a farmer, and a clay water pot. The weaver does not eat fish. The farmer will take fish but says a sack of rice is worth 'about 8 kg of fish, or maybe 10'. The potter wants fish but will be home only in the evening, and fish left in the sun all day goes bad.
(a) Which problem of barter does the weaver show?
(b) Which problem does the farmer's 'about 8 kg, or maybe 10' show?
(c) Which problem does the potter's evening timing create for Meenu?
(d) Meenu's brother says, 'Dry and salt the fish first, and all your problems are over.' Judge his advice.
questions.a: (a) Double coincidence of wants: the weaver does not want what Meenu has. (b) No common standard measure of value: they cannot fix in what proportion fish and rice should be exchanged. (c) Durability: the fish cannot be kept all day without spoiling. (d) Only partly sound: drying would help the fish last (durability) and perhaps be easier to carry, but the weaver still does not want fish and the amount for a sack of rice is still not settled; money, accepted by everybody and with prices, would remove all three problems.
s: (a) Names double coincidence of wants
(b) Names the lack of a common standard measure of value
(c) Names durability, since the fish spoils by evening
(d) Judges the advice as only partly helpful: it eases durability but not the weaver's want or the measure of value

questions.q:
Rekha lives in a village where only barter is used. She has woven one large woollen carpet, and she needs a lamp, some oil and a pair of sandals. Name the problem of barter in each case.
(a) The lamp-maker does not want a carpet at all.
(b) The oil-seller wants the carpet, but they argue for hours over how much oil it is worth.
(c) The sandal-maker would take a small piece of the carpet, but cutting it would spoil it.
(d) Rekha has to carry the heavy carpet from village to village.
(e) Rekha takes a pot of milk for the carpet from a neighbour, but the milk turns sour before she can trade it on.
questions.a: (a) Double coincidence of wants. (b) No common standard measure of value. (c) Divisibility. (d) Portability. (e) Durability.
s: (a) Double coincidence of wants
(b) Lack of a common standard measure of value
(c) Divisibility
(d) Portability
(e) Durability

questions.q: In which district of Assam is the Junbeel Mela held?
questions.a: Morigaon district of Assam, at Junbeel.

questions.q: With which ceremony does the Junbeel Mela begin?
o: The Agni Puja, the worship of fire
A feast of rice cakes for all visitors
A meeting of traders to fix prices
A boat race on the wetland
questions.a: The Agni Puja, the worship of fire, a prayer for universal wellbeing.

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the Junbeel Mela.
I. In Assamese, 'jun' means moon and 'beel' means wetland.
II. The mela is held only once every ten years.
III. Handmade goods made from forest materials of the hilly region are often exchanged with people from the plains for rice cakes.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the Junbeel Mela is a three-day annual fair.

questions.q: True or False? 'When a vendor gives new utensils for old clothes, only the household gains from the exchange.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the exchange benefits both parties: households get rid of items they no longer need, while vendors collect materials that can be resold, repurposed or recycled.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: both gain, as the vendor collects clothes to resell, repurpose or recycle

questions.q: Name any two examples of barter that the chapter says still take place today.
questions.a: Any two of: the Junbeel Mela in Assam; book exchange clubs where friends swap books; exchanging old clothes for new utensils with a visiting vendor.
s: Names a first correct example, such as the Junbeel Mela
Names a second correct example, such as book exchange or old clothes for utensils

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Junbeel Mela is described as a socio-cultural fair, not only a market.
Reason (R): Bartering at the Junbeel Mela begins early in the morning.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The mela is socio-cultural because it begins with the Agni Puja and grew from the chiefs' yearly gathering to discuss political issues and keep friendly relations; the early start of bartering does not explain this.

questions.q: At the Junbeel Mela a hill family brings ginger, wild herbs and a cane mat they made from forest materials. (a) Which of these would the chapter call a handmade good, and which are local products? (b) Why, according to the chapter, do hill families take rice cakes and other food from the plains people in return?
questions.a: (a) The cane mat is a handmade good made from natural forest materials; the ginger and wild herbs are local products (spices and herbs). (b) Rice cakes and those other foods cannot be grown in the hills.
s: Sorts the cane mat as handmade and the ginger and herbs as local products
Explains that these foods cannot be grown in the hills

questions.q: Compare the Junbeel Mela with a book exchange club on three points: (a) who takes part, (b) what is exchanged, (c) whether money is used.
questions.a: (a) The mela draws people of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities from the hills and people from the plains; a book club is a group of friends. (b) At the mela, roots, vegetables, fruit, herbs, spices and handmade forest goods are exchanged for rice cakes and other food; in the club, read books are swapped for new ones. (c) Neither uses money: both are barter.
s: Compares who takes part: hill communities and plains people versus a group of friends
Compares what is exchanged: produce and handmade goods for food versus books for books
States that neither uses money, so both are barter

questions.q:
Read the case and answer.
Ritu's family from Guwahati visits the Junbeel Mela. They arrive on the first morning, just after the Agni Puja. Ritu notes hill families with turmeric, black pepper and bamboo baskets, and plains families with bags of rice cakes. Her mother offers a hill woman ₹200 for a basket, but the woman shakes her head and points to a bag of rice cakes instead.
(a) What kind of exchange did the hill woman want, and why is it called that?
(b) Why do hill families want rice cakes, according to the chapter?
(c) When Ritu's mother offered ₹200, which function of money was she trying to use?
(d) Ritu says, 'Money is more convenient, so the mela should switch to rupees.' Judge her view.
questions.a: (a) Barter: she wanted goods for goods, with no money used. (b) Rice cakes and other such foods cannot be grown in the hills. (c) Money as a medium of exchange: she offered money as the payment for the basket. (d) Money does remove problems of barter in general, but at the mela the double coincidence of wants is already met: hill people want plains food and plains people want forest goods, and they meet at a fixed place each year. The barter is also part of a socio-cultural tradition going back centuries, so switching would lose that. A reasoned view either way that uses these points earns the mark.
s: (a) Identifies barter: goods for goods without money
(b) Explains that these foods cannot be grown in the hills
(c) Names money as a medium of exchange, offered as payment for the basket
(d) Gives a reasoned judgement using the double coincidence already met at the mela and its socio-cultural tradition

questions.q: (a) The chiefs whose yearly gathering grew into the Junbeel Mela came from tribal communities of which two states? (b) Name any two local products that are traded when bartering begins early in the morning at the mela.
questions.a: (a) Assam and Meghalaya. (b) Any two of: roots, vegetables, fruit, herbs, spices.
s: Names Assam and Meghalaya
Names two of roots, vegetables, fruit, herbs and spices

questions.q: Money is accepted as a way of making payments at a later time. Because of this, money is called a
questions.a: Standard of deferred payment.

questions.q: A shop's price board reads 'Notebook ₹45, Pen ₹15'. A shopper sees at once that one notebook is worth three pens. Which function of money lets her compare the two like this?
questions.a: Common denomination: money measures the value of goods and lets us compare them by their prices (₹45 / ₹15 = 3).

questions.q:
Match each function of money in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. Medium of exchange  2. Standard of deferred payment  3. Store of value  4. Common denomination
Column II: P. Money can be kept for a long time and used for purchases later  Q. Money is the accepted method of payment when buying and selling  R. Money measures the value of goods and services and lets us compare them by price  S. Money is accepted as a way of paying at a later time
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Medium of exchange = the accepted method of payment; standard of deferred payment = accepted for paying later; store of value = kept and used later; common denomination = measures value and allows comparison by price.

questions.q: Give two reasons from the chapter why a new system of exchange, money, was needed in place of barter.
questions.a: The types and numbers of things being exchanged grew, and the distances across which barter took place became longer, so a common medium of exchange was needed to make trade easier.
s: States that the types and numbers of things exchanged grew
States that distances of exchange became longer, so a common medium of exchange was needed

questions.q: True or False? 'Unlike wheat, money can be kept for a long time and used for buying things later, so money acts as a store of value.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The farmer's wheat would rot or be eaten by rats, but money can be kept for a longer time and used for purchases later, so the chapter calls money a store of value.
s: States the verdict: True
Explains that wheat rots or is eaten by rats while money can be kept and used later

questions.q: At a village fair, a clay pot costs ₹120, a basket ₹80 and a mat ₹200. How many baskets are worth the same as one mat and one pot together, and which function of money lets you work this out?
o: 4 baskets; money as a common denomination
4 baskets; money as a store of value
3 baskets; money as a common denomination
5 baskets; money as a medium of exchange
questions.a: 4 baskets, since (₹200 + ₹120) / ₹80 = 4; prices in money act as a common denomination that lets goods be compared.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): For the farmer, money is a better store of value than wheat.
Reason (R): Money is accepted as a way of making deferred payments.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Money stores value better because it can be kept for a long time, while wheat rots or is eaten by rats; being accepted for deferred payment is a different function.

questions.q: A school canteen lets students take lunch during the week and pay the whole amount on Friday. Diya takes lunch worth ₹35 each day from Monday to Thursday. (a) How much must she pay on Friday? (b) Which function of money does the canteen's system depend on?
questions.a: (a) ₹35 x 4 = ₹140. (b) Money as a standard of deferred payment: it is accepted as a way of paying later.
s: Works out ₹35 x 4 = ₹140
Names money as a standard of deferred payment

questions.q: The chapter opens with John Maynard Keynes's words: 'The importance of money flows from it being a link between the present and the future.' Varun says, 'Money is useful only for buying things today; it has nothing to do with the future.' Use two functions of money to show whether Varun or Keynes is right.
questions.a: Keynes is right and Varun is wrong. (1) Money is a standard of deferred payment: you can take a ₹100 book today and pay part of it later. (2) Money is a store of value: the farmer can keep money for a long time and use it for purchases later, which wheat cannot do. Both functions join today with a later time, which is the link Keynes means.
s: Uses deferred payment to show money links today with a later payment
Uses store of value to show money can be kept and spent later
Concludes that Keynes is right and Varun's claim is wrong

questions.q: On Saturday, Gopi, a vegetable seller, receives ₹1,800. He pays ₹600 to his helper as wages, keeps ₹900 in a tin to buy seeds in the sowing season three months later, and spends the rest on rice for his family. A customer also takes vegetables worth ₹120 and promises to pay next week. (a) How much did Gopi spend on rice? (b) Name the function of money shown by (i) the wages and (ii) the customer's promise. (c) Name the function of money shown by the tin. (d) If Gopi had been paid in tomatoes instead of money, which use would tomatoes serve worst over the three months, and why?
questions.a: (a) ₹1,800 - ₹600 - ₹900 = ₹300. (b) (i) Medium of exchange: money is the accepted payment for the helper's work. (ii) Standard of deferred payment: the customer pays later. (c) Store of value: the money is kept for three months and spent later. (d) Storing value in the tin for three months: tomatoes would rot long before the sowing season (the problem of durability), while money keeps.
s: Names medium of exchange for the wages and standard of deferred payment for the promise
Names store of value for the money kept in the tin
Picks storing value for three months, because tomatoes would rot (durability)

questions.q: What were the symbols punched on ancient Indian coins called?
questions.a: Rupas. The coins themselves were called karshapanas or panas.

questions.q: In which year did the Government of India adopt the ₹ sign?

Consider these statements about coins.
I. The coins we use today are made of pure copper.
II. A silver coin of the Cholas shows a tiger emblem.
III. Variations of the word 'pana' are still used for money in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: today's coins are alloys consisting largely of iron, with chromium, silicon and carbon.

questions.q: (a) What is minting? (b) In ancient kingdoms, who controlled the minting and issue of coins?
questions.a: (a) Minting is the process of producing coins. (b) The rulers of the kingdoms controlled it entirely.
s: Explains minting as the process of producing coins
States that the rulers controlled minting and issue

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In ancient India, the coins of a kingdom could be used only inside that kingdom.
Reason (R): The minting and issue of coins was controlled entirely by the rulers.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true: rulers did control the minting and issue of coins, but over time the coins of powerful rulers were accepted across various kingdoms, not just their own, which helped trade across geographies.

questions.q: The chapter's timeline of money in India marks official paper money in 1861, debit and credit cards in 1980, and UPI digital money in 2016. (a) How many years passed between official paper money and cards? (b) How many years passed between cards and UPI? (c) What do your two answers suggest about how quickly new forms of money are now arriving?
questions.a: (a) 1980 - 1861 = 119 years. (b) 2016 - 1980 = 36 years. (c) The gap has shrunk from 119 to 36 years, so new forms of money are arriving faster as technology advances.
s: Works out 1980 - 1861 = 119 years
Works out 2016 - 1980 = 36 years
Concludes that new forms are coming faster as technology advances

questions.q: Sameer says, 'Coins have always been plain metal discs with only a number stamped on them.' Do you agree? Give evidence from the chapter about ancient coins and about today's coins.
questions.a: No. Ancient coins had symbols and motifs on both sides: animals, trees, hills, kings or queens, and deities. For example, Chalukya coins had a Varaha image on one side and a three-tiered parasol on the other, and a Chola coin shows a tiger emblem. Today's coins use both Hindi and English, come in different sizes for different denominations, and special coins mark national events, such as the 2021 coin for 75 years of independence.
s: Disagrees and states that ancient coins carried motifs such as animals, trees, hills, rulers and deities
Gives a specific example, such as the Chalukya Varaha and parasol or the Chola tiger
Describes today's coins: Hindi and English, different sizes, or special coins for events

questions.q:
Read the case and answer.
A museum in Thrissur, Kerala, shows a tray of 50 old coins found along the coast. Of these, 30 are gold coins with the heads of Roman kings, 15 are silver coins with small symbols punched on them, and 5 are coins made of a mix of silver and copper. A label calls the silver and the silver-copper coins Indian coins.
(a) The Roman coins show a king's head on one side. Using the chapter's glossary, what is that side of a coin called?
(b) How many coins on the tray are Indian, and what percentage of the tray is this?
(c) How many Roman gold coins are there on the tray for every punch-marked silver coin?
(d) A visitor says, 'Most of the coins on this tray are Indian, so this coast had little to do with lands across the sea.' Use your answers to (b) and (c) and the chapter to judge this view.
questions.a: (a) The obverse: the side bearing the head or principal design. (b) 15 + 5 = 20 Indian coins; 20 / 50 x 100 = 40%. (c) 30 / 15 = 2 Roman gold coins for every silver coin. (d) The view is wrong on both counts. Only 40% of the coins are Indian, while 60% (30 of 50) are Roman, twice as many as the silver coins, so 'most are Indian' is false. And the chapter says Roman gold coins found in Kerala and Tamil Nadu throw light on southern India's trade with the rest of the world, so a tray where Roman coins are the largest group points to strong contact across the sea, not little.
s: (a) Names the side as the obverse
(b) Works out 20 Indian coins, 20 / 50 x 100 = 40%
(c) Works out 30 / 15 = 2 Roman coins per silver coin
(d) Rejects the view: 60% are Roman, not Indian, and Roman coins in Kerala and Tamil Nadu show trade with the rest of the world

questions.q: Your class is asked to design a special coin to mark an important national event, as India did for 75 years of independence in 2021. Using the chapter, describe and give a reason for: (a) the metal it should be made of; (b) the languages it should carry; (c) a motif for the obverse and one for the reverse, linked to the motifs on ancient Indian coins; (d) why it should be a coin rather than a paper note if its value is small; (e) how your coin, like the 2021 one, keeps alive an old tradition of coins showing what a people value.
questions.a: (a) An alloy consisting largely of iron, with chromium, silicon and carbon, like today's coins, because an alloy makes a coin strong. (b) Hindi and English, as on every coin today. (c) For example, a national symbol or leader on the obverse (the head side) and a nature motif such as a tree, an animal or hills on the reverse, as ancient coins carried animals, trees, hills, kings and deities. (d) Coins are used for smaller denominations and paper notes for higher ones. (e) Ancient coins carried symbols and motifs important to their rulers and people; a special coin marking a national event continues that practice.
s: (a) Chooses an iron-based alloy and gives the reason that alloys make coins strong
(b) Chooses Hindi and English, as on today's coins
(c) Gives an obverse and a reverse motif linked to ancient motifs such as animals, trees, hills or rulers
(d) Explains that coins are used for smaller denominations
(e) Links the special coin to the ancient practice of coins carrying meaningful motifs

questions.q:
In an ancient story, three kingdoms lie side by side: a powerful kingdom P and two small kingdoms Q and R. As the chapter describes, the coins of the powerful ruler are accepted in all three kingdoms, while Q's coins are used only inside Q. A cloth merchant of Q sells his cloth and may take payment in one of two ways: Offer 1, 50 coins of Q; Offer 2, 50 coins of P, which are worth the same in Q. On his trip he must spend 20 coins in kingdom P and 15 coins in kingdom R before returning home to Q.
(a) With Offer 1, how many of the 35 coins he needs on his trip can he spend in P and R? Why?
(b) With Offer 2, how many coins does he bring home after the trip, and can he use them in Q?
(c) Which offer should he take? Give a reason.
(d) What does this story show about what the coins of powerful rulers did for trade, according to the chapter?
questions.a: (a) None of them: Q's coins are used only inside Q, so he cannot pay in P or R with them. (b) 50 - 20 - 15 = 15 coins; yes, the powerful ruler's coins are accepted in Q as well. (c) Offer 2: the same coins pay for all his purchases in P and R and still work at home, while Offer 1 leaves him unable to buy anything on the trip. (d) Over time the coins of powerful rulers were accepted across various kingdoms and not just their own, and this facilitated trade across geographies.
s: (a) States he can spend none, as Q's coins work only inside Q
(b) Works out 50 - 20 - 15 = 15 coins and says they can be used in Q
(c) Chooses Offer 2 with a reason based on where each coin is accepted
(d) Coins of powerful rulers were accepted across kingdoms, which facilitated trade across geographies

questions.q: According to the chapter, in which country was paper money first used?
questions.a: China; it was introduced in India in the late 18th century.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of digital money?
o: Paying a shopkeeper through UPI on a mobile phone
questions.a: Paying through UPI on a mobile phone: digital money is intangible, electronic money, while coins, notes and shells can be touched.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. Reserve Bank of India  2. QR code  3. Denominations  4. Currency
Column II: P. Black and white squares, readable by smartphones, holding the receiver's bank account details  Q. The central authority that controls the issue of currency in India  R. The system of money used in a particular country  S. The units in which coins and paper notes are classified
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: RBI = the central authority that controls the issue of currency; QR code = squares holding the receiver's bank details; denominations = the units in which coins and notes are classified; currency = the system of money used in a country.

questions.q:
Read the case and answer.
At closing time, Farhan counts the cash box of his family's medical shop in Nagpur. It holds 4 notes of ₹500, 6 notes of ₹100, 10 coins of ₹10 and 20 coins of ₹5. He puts the notes in one bundle and the coins in a small bag, ready to take to the bank the next morning.
(a) What is the total value of the notes?
(b) What is the total value of the coins?
(c) Which body controls the issue of currency in India today, and may anybody else issue it?
(d) Why are the larger amounts in the box in notes and the smaller ones in coins?
questions.a: (a) 4 x ₹500 + 6 x ₹100 = ₹2,000 + ₹600 = ₹2,600. (b) 10 x ₹10 + 20 x ₹5 = ₹100 + ₹100 = ₹200. (c) The Reserve Bank of India (RBI); it is not legal for anybody other than the RBI to issue currency. (d) In India, coins are used for smaller denominations and paper currency for higher denominations.
s: (c) Names the RBI and states that nobody else may legally issue currency
(d) States that coins are for smaller denominations and paper notes for higher ones

questions.q: True or False? 'When a customer pays a fruit seller by scanning his QR code, the money first goes to the Reserve Bank of India, which then passes it on to the seller.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The payment goes directly into the seller's bank account: these methods transfer money directly from one person's bank account into another. The RBI's role in the chapter is to control the issue of currency.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: the money moves directly from the buyer's bank account into the seller's

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Krishnappa's customers can pay him straight into his bank account without being told his bank account details.
Reason (R): The QR code on his card contains information about the receiver's bank account and can be read by their mobile phones.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: the QR code carries the receiver's bank account information, so scanning it with a phone sends the payment directly into Krishnappa's account.

questions.q: As coins came to be used for every kind of exchange, from buying vegetables to buying land, problems arose. (a) Name the two problems the chapter describes. (b) Explain why these problems were worst for large payments such as land. (c) Paper money solved them, yet coins are still used. Explain why, using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) It became difficult to carry a large number of coins, and storing the coins also became a problem. (b) A large payment such as land needs a very large number of coins, so carrying and storing them is hardest then. (c) Coins are still used for smaller denominations, while paper currency is used for higher ones, so each fits a different size of payment.
s: Names the difficulty of carrying and of storing large numbers of coins
Explains that large payments need very many coins, making these problems worst
Explains that coins remain for smaller denominations and notes for higher ones

questions.q: Class 7B is collecting ₹60 from each of its 35 students for a museum trip. The bus company must be paid the full amount into its bank account. Students may pay in ₹5 coins, in ₹20 notes, or by UPI into the class teacher's bank account by scanning her QR code. (a) What is the total amount to be collected? (b) If every student paid in ₹5 coins, how many coins would the teacher have to count, carry and store? Which problem described in the chapter does this show? (c) If every student paid in ₹20 notes instead, how many notes would there be? (d) In fact 25 students pay by UPI and the other 10 pay in ₹20 notes. How much reaches the teacher's bank account directly, and how many notes must she carry to the bank? (e) Using your working and the chapter, judge which way of collecting is best for paying the bus company, and say why the teacher should still accept some notes.
questions.a: (a) 35 x 60 = ₹2,100. (b) 2,100 / 5 = 420 coins; this is the chapter's problem that a large number of coins is difficult to carry and to store. (c) 2,100 / 20 = 105 notes. (d) 25 x 60 = ₹1,500 reaches her account directly; the other 10 x 60 = ₹600 is 600 / 20 = 30 notes to carry to the bank. (e) UPI is best: the money moves directly from one bank account into another, so there are no coins or notes to count, carry, store or deposit before paying the bus company; 420 coins is the worst, and notes are in between (105 instead of 420). She should still accept notes because a payment by UPI needs a bank account and a mobile phone, which not every family may use.
s: (a) Works out 35 x 60 = ₹2,100
(b) Works out 420 coins and names the difficulty of carrying and storing many coins
(c) Works out 105 notes
(d) Works out ₹1,500 by UPI and 30 notes (₹600)
(e) Judges UPI best using the working and direct bank-to-bank transfer, and gives a reason to still accept notes

questions.q:
Imagine buying a sack of rice in four different ways: (1) in a barter village, paying with a goat; (2) in an ancient kingdom, paying with silver panas; (3) paying a large bill with paper notes instead of a heap of coins; (4) paying by UPI from a mobile phone.
(a) State two difficulties of way (1).
(b) For ways (2) and (3), state what each removed compared with the way before it.
(c) State what way (4) needs that the other three do not.
(d) A weekly hill market has no bank branch and no mobile network, and the rice seller there wants nothing that a buyer has to offer except money. Which of the four ways can a buyer use there, and which would you choose for one sack? Give reasons from your answers to (a)-(c).
questions.a: (a) Double coincidence of wants: the rice seller must want a goat; divisibility: a goat cannot be split to match one sack. (b) Panas: coins issued by the ruler are accepted for payment, so no double coincidence of wants is needed; paper notes: they remove the difficulty of carrying and storing a large number of coins. (c) UPI transfers money directly from one person's bank account into another, scanned with a mobile phone, so it needs bank accounts and a working phone connection. (d) Way (1) fails because the seller does not want a goat and the goat cannot be divided; way (4) fails because there is no mobile network. So the buyer must pay in coins or notes; for a whole sack, notes are the sensible choice because paper currency is used for higher amounts and avoids carrying many coins.
s: (a) Names double coincidence of wants and divisibility for the goat
(b) Coins remove the need for double coincidence; notes remove carrying and storing many coins
(c) UPI needs bank accounts and a mobile phone to move money directly between accounts
(d) Rules out barter and UPI with reasons and chooses notes (or coins) for the sack with a reason

questions.q: A tourist from Japan in Delhi offers a tea seller a Japanese note, and the tea seller politely refuses it. (a) Using the chapter's meaning of 'currency', explain why. (b) Name one coin and one paper note denomination of Indian currency from the chapter's list.
questions.a: (a) Currency is the system of money used in a particular country; the Japanese note is Japan's currency, while in India the rupee coins and notes are the currency, so the tea seller does not accept it. (b) For example, a ₹5 coin and a ₹200 note (any coin from 50 paisa, ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20 and any note from ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500, ₹1000).
s: Explains that currency is the money system of a particular country, so Japanese notes are not India's currency
Names one coin and one note denomination from the chapter's list
